title: Frequency of element query
description:
Given an integer array A of N elements and an array B of Q queries. For each query B[i], return the frequency of B[i] in A.

Problem Constraints
1 ≤ N, Q ≤ 10^5
1 ≤ A[i], B[i] ≤ 10^9

Example
A = [1,2,1,1], B = [1,2] → [3, 1].
story: Build freq HashMap in O(N); each query is O(1) average.
plain: Brute: per query, scan A — O(N*Q). Optimal: one pass to build HashMap<value, count>, then answer each query with map.getOrDefault(B[i], 0).
tale: Pre-bake a phonebook of names→counts; answer 'how many John?' instantly instead of re-counting the room each time.
pitfalls: A query value may not be in the map, so use `getOrDefault(B[i], 0)` not `get` or you get a null crash.
Values go up to 1e9, so don't index a plain `int[]` by value; you need a HashMap.
Build the freq map fully before answering any query, not while you scan queries.

solutions.label: Brute — Scan per Query
solutions.plain: Per query, walk A counting matches.
solutions.tale: Recount the room for every name.
approach: For each query q in B: walk A, count occurrences of q.
Push count to result.
solutions.pseudocode: for q in B: c=0; for x in A: if x==q: c++; res.add(c)

solutions.label: Optimal — HashMap Frequency
solutions.plain: Build one freq map; query in O(1).
approach: Build HashMap<Integer, Integer> freq from A using merge / getOrDefault.
For each query: result[i] = freq.getOrDefault(B[i], 0).
solutions.pseudocode: freq[A[i]]++; for q in B: res.add(freq.get(q) or 0)

data.footer: Frequency map of A then 2 queries.

script.label: SETUP
script.overlay: Why HashMap? Values can be up to 1e9 — an int[] indexed by value won't fit.

script.label: DONE
script.overlay: Tip: use merge or getOrDefault to avoid NullPointerException.

title: Count Distinct Elements
description:
Given an array A of N integers, return the number of distinct elements.

Problem Constraints
1 ≤ N ≤ 10^5
1 ≤ A[i] ≤ 10^9

Example
A = [3, 4, 3, 6, 6] → 3 (distinct = {3,4,6}).
story: Drop everything into a HashSet; answer is set.size().
plain: Brute: sort and count groups O(N log N). Optimal: HashSet insertion + size() in O(N) average.
tale: Put each marble in a labelled jar; the number of non-empty jars is the answer.
pitfalls: You want the count of distinct values, so return `seen.size()`, not the array length.
Values reach 1e9, so a boolean array won't fit; use a HashSet.
Empty array should give 0, so make sure size() handles that (it does).

solutions.label: Brute — Sort & Count Groups
solutions.plain: Sort the array; count positions where value differs from previous.
solutions.tale: Line everyone up, then count colour changes.
approach: Copy & sort.
distinct = (N > 0 ? 1 : 0); for i = 1..N-1 if A[i] != A[i-1] → distinct++.
solutions.pseudocode: sort(A); count = 1 + Σ_{i=1..N-1} (A[i]!=A[i-1])
solutions.story: OK but O(N log N) vs hashing's O(N).

solutions.label: Optimal — HashSet
solutions.plain: Add to a HashSet; size() is the answer.
solutions.tale: Drop each element into a unique-by-construction bag.
approach: Set<Integer> seen = new HashSet<>();
for x in A: seen.add(x);
return seen.size().
solutions.pseudocode: set = HashSet; add each; return set.size()
solutions.story: Optimal. The HashSet absorbs duplicates automatically.

script.label: SETUP
script.overlay: Why a set? Insertions are O(1) average and duplicates are silently ignored.

title: First Repeating element
description:
Given an integer array A, return the first repeating element (the element that appears more than once and whose FIRST occurrence has the smallest index). If no repeating element exists, return -1.

Problem Constraints
1 ≤ N ≤ 10^5
1 ≤ A[i] ≤ 10^9

Example
A = [10, 5, 3, 4, 3, 5, 6] → 5 (5 repeats and its first occurrence is at index 1, before 3's first at index 2).
story: Two passes: (1) build freq map; (2) walk A left-to-right and return the first element with freq > 1.
plain: Brute O(N²) per element. Optimal: 1 pass to build HashMap<value, count>, then 1 pass to scan in order and return first key with count > 1.
tale: Take attendance to know who has a twin in the room, then point to the FIRST person whose twin you spotted.
pitfalls: First repeating means smallest first-occurrence index, so scan the array in order, not the map (map order is undefined).
Build the whole freq map first, then do the order scan; don't try to do both in one loop.
Return -1 if nothing repeats; don't forget that case.

solutions.label: Brute — Pairwise Search
solutions.plain: For each i, scan j > i for a match.
approach: For i = 0..N-1: for j = i+1..N-1: if A[i]==A[j] → return A[i].
Return -1.
solutions.pseudocode: for i; for j>i: if A[i]==A[j]: return A[i]; return -1

solutions.label: Optimal — Frequency Map + Linear Scan
solutions.plain: Build freq, then scan in order for freq > 1.
approach: Build HashMap<Integer, Integer> freq from A.
For x in A in order: if freq.get(x) > 1 → return x.
Return -1.
solutions.pseudocode: freq=build; for x in A: if freq[x]>1: return x; return -1
solutions.story: Optimal. Two linear passes, total O(N).

data.footer: First repeating element by first-occurrence index.

script.label: SETUP
script.overlay: Why two passes? Pass 1 = counts; Pass 2 = order. HashMap iteration order is undefined, so walk the array.

title: Sub-array with 0 sum
description:
Given an array A of N integers, return 1 if there exists a (contiguous) sub-array with sum 0; else return 0.

Problem Constraints
1 ≤ N ≤ 10^5
-10^9 ≤ A[i] ≤ 10^9

Example
A = [1, -2, 1, 2] → 1 ([1,-2,1] sums to 0).
A = [5, 6, -3, 4] → 0.
story: Walk prefix sums; if any prefix repeats OR a prefix equals 0, found.
plain: Brute O(N²) — try all subarrays. Optimal: running prefix sum + HashSet of seen prefixes (include 0 sentinel). If currentSum is already in the set, subarray strictly after the previous occurrence sums to 0.
tale: Tally as you walk. If you ever return to a previously-seen total, the steps between were zero net.
pitfalls: Seed the set with 0 first, or a zero-sum starting at index 0 gets missed.
Sums can hit ±1e14, so use a `Set<Long>`, not int, to dodge overflow.
Check `contains(sum)` before adding the current sum, not after.

solutions.label: Brute — All Subarrays
solutions.plain: Double loop; running sum reset per start.
approach: For l = 0..N-1: s = 0; for r = l..N-1: s += A[r]; if s == 0 → return 1.
Return 0.
solutions.pseudocode: for l; s=0; for r>=l: s+=A[r]; if s==0 return 1

solutions.label: Optimal — Prefix Sum + HashSet
solutions.plain: Running sum; check if it's been seen (including 0).
approach: Set<Long> seen = new HashSet<>(); seen.add(0L); long sum = 0.
For x in A: sum += x; if seen.contains(sum) → return 1; seen.add(sum).
Return 0.
solutions.pseudocode: seen={0}; sum=0; for x: sum+=x; if sum in seen: return 1; seen.add(sum)
solutions.story: Optimal. Use long to dodge overflow.

script.label: SETUP
script.overlay: Why include 0? So a subarray starting at index 0 with sum 0 is detected (sum == 0 matches the sentinel).

script.label: i=0: sum=1, not in seen → add
i=1: sum=-1, not in seen → add

title: Common Elements
description:
Given two arrays A and B, find their common elements respecting multiplicity. If an element x appears p times in A and q times in B, it should appear min(p, q) times in the output. Return the output in any (consistent) order — typically the order in which they appear in B.

Problem Constraints
1 ≤ |A|, |B| ≤ 10^5
1 ≤ A[i], B[i] ≤ 10^9

Example
A = [1, 2, 2, 1], B = [2, 3, 1, 2] → [2, 1, 2] (B-order intersection).
story: Build freq map of A; walk B and for each x present in the map, emit it and decrement.
plain: Brute O(N*M) cross-search. Optimal: HashMap<value, count> of A; for each x in B: if count > 0, output x and decrement count. Order follows B.
tale: Hand A a bag of coloured marbles with counts. Walk B; each time you find a colour with stock, give one back.
pitfalls: Use a freq map, not a set, or you lose multiplicity and `min(p,q)` counts break.
Decrement the count each time you emit, so you don't over-report a value.
Walk B to build output; the answer order follows B, not A.

solutions.label: Brute — Cross Search with Used Flags
solutions.plain: For each x in B, scan A for an unused match.
approach: boolean[] used = new boolean[A.length].
For x in B: scan A; first j with !used[j] && A[j]==x → mark, append.
Return list.
solutions.pseudocode: used=false; for x in B: for j: if !used[j] and A[j]==x: used[j]=true; out.add(x); break

solutions.label: Optimal — Frequency Map of A
solutions.plain: Map of A's counts; walk B and emit while count > 0.
approach: Build freq map of A.
List out = new ArrayList<>().
For x in B: int c = freq.getOrDefault(x, 0); if c > 0 → out.add(x); freq.put(x, c - 1).
Return out as int[].
solutions.pseudocode: freq=A; for x in B: c=freq[x]; if c>0: out.add(x); freq[x]=c-1
solutions.story: Optimal. Order matches B which most graders expect.

script.label: SETUP
script.overlay: Why a multimap (freq)? A simple set would lose multiplicity — [2,2] vs [2] would collide.

title: Count Unique Elements
description:
Given an array A, count the number of elements that appear EXACTLY once in A.

Problem Constraints
1 ≤ N ≤ 10^5
1 ≤ A[i] ≤ 10^9

Example
A = [1, 2, 3, 1, 2, 4] → 2 ({3, 4} are unique).
story: Build freq map; count entries with value == 1.
plain: Brute O(N²). Optimal: HashMap freq pass + count of entries with count == 1.
tale: Take attendance; count seats with exactly one person.
pitfalls: Unique here means frequency exactly 1, not distinct values; don't confuse the two.
Count map entries where the value is 1, not the number of keys.
A value appearing twice counts as zero unique, not one.

solutions.label: Brute — Pairwise Check
solutions.plain: For each i, count occurrences in A. If 1, ans++.
approach: ans=0; for i: c=0; for j: if A[j]==A[i]: c++; if c==1: ans++.
solutions.pseudocode: for i: c=count(A[i] in A); if c==1: ans++

solutions.label: Optimal — Frequency Map
solutions.plain: Build freq, count entries with value 1.
approach: Build HashMap<Integer, Integer> freq.
Count entries where value == 1.
solutions.pseudocode: freq=build; return count(e.value==1)

data.footer: Count of elements appearing exactly once.

title: Count Subarray Zero Sum
description:
Given an array A, count the number of contiguous sub-arrays whose sum is zero. Return the count modulo 10^9 + 7.

Problem Constraints
1 ≤ N ≤ 10^5
-10^9 ≤ A[i] ≤ 10^9

Example
A = [1, -1, 2, -2] → 3 ([1,-1], [2,-2], [1,-1,2,-2]).
story: Running prefix sum; HashMap<prefix, count of times seen>. For each new prefix, add count_of(currentSum) — number of earlier positions where same prefix appeared.
plain: Brute O(N²) over all subarrays. Optimal: HashMap of prefix-sum frequencies, sentinel {0 → 1} so a subarray starting at index 0 is counted, accumulate getOrDefault(currentSum, 0) before incrementing the map.
tale: Every time the running tally returns to a past value, the steps between net to zero — count all such return-pairs.
pitfalls: Seed the map with `{0:1}`, or subarrays starting at index 0 are undercounted.
Add `getOrDefault(sum,0)` to the answer before you bump the count for `sum`.
Prefix sums can overflow int, so key the map with `Long`; and apply the mod.

solutions.label: Brute — Pair-Sum All Subarrays
solutions.plain: Try every (l, r).
approach: ans = 0; for l: s = 0; for r ≥ l: s += A[r]; if s == 0: ans = (ans+1) % MOD.
solutions.pseudocode: for l; for r: s+=A[r]; if s==0: ans++

solutions.label: Optimal — Prefix Sum + HashMap
solutions.plain: Count how many times each prefix sum has appeared; matches contribute pairs.
approach: Map<Long, Integer> seen = new HashMap<>(); seen.put(0L, 1); long sum = 0; long ans = 0.
For x in A: sum += x; ans += seen.getOrDefault(sum, 0); seen.merge(sum, 1, Integer::sum).
Return (int)(ans % MOD).
solutions.pseudocode: seen={0:1}; sum=0; for x: sum+=x; ans+=seen[sum]; seen[sum]++

script.label: SETUP
script.overlay: Why a count map? If a prefix sum has appeared k times before, the current index creates k new zero-sum subarrays — one per past occurrence.

script.label: i=3: sum=0, seen[0]=2 → +2
script.msg: ans = 3 (one for the [2,-2] subarray, one for the whole array).

title: Check Pair Sum
description:
Given an array A and integer B, return 1 if there exists a pair (i, j) with i ≠ j and A[i] + A[j] == B; else return 0.

Problem Constraints
1 ≤ N ≤ 10^5
-10^9 ≤ A[i], B ≤ 10^9

Example
A = [3, 5, 1, 2], B = 6 → 1 (5+1).
A = [1, 2, 3], B = 8 → 0.
story: Single-pass with HashSet of seen values; for each x, check if (B − x) was already seen.
plain: Brute O(N²) over pairs. Optimal: walk once, maintain HashSet; on each x, if (B − x) ∈ set → return 1; else add x to set. O(N) average.
tale: Walk a line of partygoers; before greeting each one, ask 'has my complement been here?'.
pitfalls: Check `contains(B - x)` first, then add x; otherwise a single x can pair with itself.
`B - x` can overflow int with values near 1e9, so compute it as `long`.
Return 0 if no pair is found, and require i ≠ j (the check-before-insert handles it).

solutions.label: Brute — All Pairs
solutions.plain: Try every pair.
approach: For i, for j > i: if A[i] + A[j] == B → return 1. Return 0.
solutions.pseudocode: for i; for j>i: if A[i]+A[j]==B: return 1

solutions.label: Optimal — Single Pass HashSet
solutions.plain: Check complement in set before inserting.
solutions.tale: Ask 'is my complement here?' as you walk.
approach: Set<Integer> seen = new HashSet<>().
For x in A: if seen.contains(B − x) → return 1; seen.add(x).
Return 0.
solutions.pseudocode: for x: if (B-x) in seen: return 1; seen.add(x)

script.label: SETUP
script.overlay: Order matters: check complement first, THEN insert — otherwise B=2*x case would self-match.

title: Count Pair Difference
description:
Given an array A of N integers and integer B, count the number of pairs (i, j) with i ≠ j such that |A[i] − A[j]| == B. Unordered pairs — (i, j) is same as (j, i). Return count modulo 10^9 + 7.

Problem Constraints
1 ≤ N ≤ 10^5
-10^9 ≤ A[i] ≤ 10^9
0 ≤ B ≤ 10^9

Example
A = [1, 5, 3, 4, 2], B = 2 → 3 (pairs {5,3}, {3,1}, {4,2}).
story: Two-pass: build full freq, then for every distinct value x add freq[x] * freq[x+B]. Special-case B == 0 with C(freq[x], 2).
plain: Brute O(N²). Optimal two-pass: (1) build HashMap<value, count> of A; (2) for each entry x add freq[x] * freq[x + B] to ans — captures both directions of |a−b|=B at once. Special case B == 0: result is Σ C(freq[x], 2).
tale: Walking a line; ask 'how many people behind me are exactly B less than me?' and add to the tally.
pitfalls: B == 0 is a special case; count `C(freq[x],2)` per value instead of `freq[x]*freq[x+B]`.
Only look at `x + B` (not also `x - B`), or every pair gets counted twice.
Counts multiply up large, so use `long` keys/values and apply the mod.

solutions.label: Brute — All Pairs
solutions.plain: Try every pair, count A[i] − A[j] == B.
approach: ans = 0; for i, for j > i: if A[i] − A[j] == B → ans++.
solutions.pseudocode: for i; for j>i: if A[i]-A[j]==B: ans++

solutions.label: Optimal — Two-Pass Frequency Map
solutions.plain: Build freq, then sum freq[x] * freq[x+B] over distinct x.
solutions.tale: Histogram first, then count partner pairs.
approach: Build HashMap<Long, Long> freq from A.
If B == 0: ans = Σ C(freq[x], 2) for each x; return ans % MOD.
Else: for each entry x: ans += freq[x] * freq.getOrDefault(x + B, 0L). Return ans % MOD.
solutions.pseudocode: freq=build; B==0 ? Σ C(freq[x],2) : Σ freq[x]*freq[x+B]
solutions.story: Optimal. Captures |a−b|=B in one direction (x as smaller, x+B as larger) so no double-count.

script.label: SETUP
script.overlay: Why two-pass? Single-pass complement-before-insert misses pairs where the larger value appears first (e.g. 5 then 3).

script.label: x=2: partner = freq[4] = 1 → +1
script.overlay: No double-count: each pair {a, b} (a

title: Subarray Sum Equals K
description:
Given an array A of N integers and integer B (= K), count the number of contiguous subarrays with sum exactly equal to B.

Problem Constraints
1 ≤ N ≤ 10^5
-10^3 ≤ A[i] ≤ 10^3 (typical)
-10^9 ≤ B ≤ 10^9

Example
A = [1, 0, 1], B = 1 → 4 ([1], [0,1], [1,0], [1,0,1] has sum 2 — recount: actually [1] start 0, [1] start 2, [0,1] start 1, [1,0] start 0 sum 1) Standard answer: 4.
story: Walk prefix sums; ans += count of (currentSum − B) seen before.
plain: Brute O(N²). Optimal: HashMap<prefix sum, count>. Init {0:1}. For each step: ans += map[currentSum − B], then map[currentSum]++.
tale: Each prefix sum is a checkpoint; pair every current checkpoint with all past checkpoints exactly B below.
pitfalls: Seed the map with `{0:1}`, or subarrays whose sum equals B from index 0 are missed.
Add `map[sum - B]` to the answer before incrementing `map[sum]`.
A[i] can be negative, so two pointers won't work; use the prefix-sum map, keyed with `Long`.

solutions.label: Brute — All Subarrays
solutions.plain: Sum every subarray, compare with B.
approach: For l: s=0; for r ≥ l: s += A[r]; if s == B → ans++.
solutions.pseudocode: for l; for r: s+=A[r]; if s==B: ans++

solutions.label: Optimal — Prefix Sum + HashMap
solutions.plain: Count of (sum − B) seen earlier.
approach: Map<Long, Integer> seen = new HashMap<>(); seen.put(0L, 1); long sum = 0; int ans = 0.
For x in A: sum += x; ans += seen.getOrDefault(sum − B, 0); seen.merge(sum, 1, Integer::sum).
Return ans.
solutions.pseudocode: seen={0:1}; sum=0; for x: sum+=x; ans+=seen[sum-B]; seen[sum]++

script.label: SETUP
script.overlay: Why seed seen[0]=1? So a prefix equal to B (subarray starting at index 0) is counted.

title: Distinct Numbers in Window
description:
Given an array A of N integers and a window size B, return an array of length N−B+1 where each entry is the number of distinct integers in the corresponding window A[i..i+B−1].

Problem Constraints
1 ≤ B ≤ N ≤ 10^5
1 ≤ A[i] ≤ 10^9

Example
A = [1, 2, 1, 3, 4, 3], B = 3 → [2, 3, 3, 2].
story: Sliding window; HashMap<value, count> maintained as the window moves. distinct = map.size() (drop keys when count → 0).
plain: Brute O(N*B). Optimal: build the first window, then slide one step at a time — increment the new entrant, decrement the departing entry (remove key if its count hits 0). Emit map.size() after each step.
tale: A moving spotlight on a parade; tally how many distinct costumes are visible at each moment.
pitfalls: When a value's count drops to 0, remove the key, or `map.size()` counts ghosts.
Build the first window separately, then slide; don't rebuild each window.
Add the incoming element and remove the outgoing `A[i-B]` each step, in that order.

solutions.label: Brute — Recount Each Window
solutions.plain: For each i, build a fresh set of A[i..i+B-1].
approach: For i = 0..N−B: build Set of A[i..i+B−1]; push set.size().
solutions.pseudocode: for i: set={A[i..i+B-1]}; out.add(set.size())

solutions.label: Optimal — Sliding Window with HashMap
solutions.plain: One-pass maintain freq map for the window.
solutions.tale: Move the window, tweak the counts.
approach: Build initial window: for i = 0..B−1 → freq.merge(A[i], 1, +).
out[0] = freq.size().
For i = B..N−1: freq.merge(A[i], 1, +); decrement A[i−B] (remove if 0); out[i−B+1] = freq.size().
solutions.pseudocode: build first window; slide: add new, remove old (drop key if 0); emit size
solutions.story: Optimal. Always remember to drop zero-count keys.

data.footer: Sliding window of size B=3, count distinct.

script.label: SETUP
script.overlay: Why drop zero-count keys? map.size() counts all keys, not non-zero values; ghosts inflate the count.

title: Longest Subarray Zero Sum
description:
Given an array A of N integers, return the length of the longest contiguous sub-array whose sum is zero. If no such sub-array exists, return 0.

Problem Constraints
1 ≤ N ≤ 10^5
-10^9 ≤ A[i] ≤ 10^9

Example
A = [1, -2, 1, 2] → 3 ([1,-2,1]).
A = [3, 2, -1] → 0.
story: Map<prefixSum, EARLIEST index>. If currentSum was seen at index k, subarray (k+1..i) sums to 0; length = i − k. Special case: if currentSum is 0 at index i, length = i + 1.
plain: Brute O(N²). Optimal: prefix sum + HashMap of FIRST occurrence of each prefix; do NOT overwrite. If sum == 0 at index i → maxLen = max(maxLen, i+1). Else if seen → maxLen = max(maxLen, i − seen[sum]).
tale: First time you reach a tally, plant a flag. Next time you pass it, measure the stretch back to the flag — longest such stretch is the answer.
pitfalls: Store only the FIRST index of each prefix sum; never overwrite it or the stretch shrinks.
When `sum == 0` the length is `i + 1`, a separate case from the map lookup.
Prefix sums can overflow, so key the map with `Long`; return 0 if none found.

solutions.label: Brute — All Subarrays
solutions.plain: Try every subarray, track max length when sum == 0.
approach: best = 0; for l: s = 0; for r ≥ l: s += A[r]; if s == 0 → best = max(best, r−l+1).
solutions.pseudocode: for l; for r: s+=A[r]; if s==0: best=max(best,r-l+1)

solutions.label: Optimal — Prefix Sum + Earliest-Index Map
solutions.plain: Store first occurrence of each prefix sum; max stretch back to it.
approach: Map<Long, Integer> firstIndex = new HashMap<>(); long sum = 0; int best = 0.
For i = 0..N−1: sum += A[i]; if sum == 0 → best = max(best, i+1).
Else if firstIndex.containsKey(sum) → best = max(best, i − firstIndex.get(sum)).
Else firstIndex.put(sum, i).
solutions.pseudocode: for i: sum+=A[i]; if sum==0: best=max(best,i+1); elif sum in map: best=max(best,i-map[sum]); else map[sum]=i
solutions.story: Optimal. Trick = NEVER overwrite the first index.

script.label: SETUP
script.overlay: Why earliest only? To maximise (i − firstIndex[sum]) you want firstIndex as small as possible.

title: Count Pair Sum
description:
Given an array A of N integers and integer B, count the number of (unordered) pairs (i, j) with i ≠ j such that A[i] + A[j] == B. The pair (i, j) is the same as (j, i) and counted once. Return count modulo 10^9 + 7.

Problem Constraints
1 ≤ N ≤ 10^5
1 ≤ A[i], B ≤ 10^9

Example
A = [3, 5, 1, 2], B = 8 → 1 (3+5).
A = [1, 2, 1, 2], B = 3 → 4 ((1,2) pairs across indices).
story: Walk once. For each x, ans += freq[B − x]; then freq[x]++. Enforces i < j and handles duplicates correctly.
plain: Brute O(N²) over pairs. Optimal: HashMap<value, count>. Single pass: pairs += freq.getOrDefault(B − x, 0) BEFORE inserting x. The 'add before insert' ordering ensures each pair is counted exactly once.
tale: Walk a queue; each person asks 'how many people behind me sum with me to B?'.
pitfalls: Add `freq[B - x]` before inserting x, so each pair is counted once and i < j holds.
Duplicates matter; use a freq map so repeated values pair up the right number of times.
Count grows large, so accumulate in `long` and apply the mod at the end.

solutions.label: Brute — All Pairs
solutions.plain: Loop i, j > i.
approach: ans = 0; for i, j > i: if A[i] + A[j] == B → ans++.
solutions.pseudocode: for i; for j>i: if A[i]+A[j]==B: ans++

solutions.label: Optimal — Single Pass HashMap
solutions.plain: Accumulate freq[B−x] before inserting x.
approach: Map<Integer, Integer> freq = new HashMap<>(); long count = 0.
For x in A: count += freq.getOrDefault(B − x, 0); freq.merge(x, 1, Integer::sum).
Return (int)(count % MOD).
solutions.pseudocode: for x: count += freq[B-x]; freq[x]++
solutions.story: Optimal. Correctly handles duplicates and i<j.

script.label: SETUP
script.overlay: Why complement-before-insert? Guarantees i

title: Subarray with given sum
subTopic: Sliding Window (positive ints) OR Prefix Sum Map
description:
Given an array A of POSITIVE integers and integer B, return the FIRST contiguous sub-array whose sum equals B (smallest start index). If no such sub-array exists, return an array containing a single -1.

Problem Constraints
1 ≤ N ≤ 10^5
1 ≤ A[i] ≤ 10^9
1 ≤ B ≤ 10^9

Example
A = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], B = 5 → [2, 3].
A = [5, 10, 20, 100, 105], B = 110 → [-1].
story: All positive ⇒ shrink window when sum exceeds B (two pointers, O(N)). Alternative: prefix-sum + HashMap (works for negatives too).
plain: Brute O(N²) over subarrays. Optimal (positives only): two pointers l, r; expand r adding to sum; while sum > B shrink from l; if sum == B → return A[l..r]. For first occurrence: take the smallest l that hits sum == B.
tale: Inflate a balloon (advance r) until it overshoots, then deflate from the back (advance l) until it fits — perfectly positive-only logic.
pitfalls: Two pointers only work because all values are positive; negatives would break the shrink logic.
Return `[-1]` (single element) when nothing matches, not an empty array.
Use `long` for the running sum, and return the FIRST match (smallest start index).

solutions.label: Brute — All Subarrays
solutions.plain: Try every (l, r).
approach: For l: s = 0; for r ≥ l: s += A[r]; if s == B → return A[l..r]; if s > B → break (positives).
Return [-1].
solutions.pseudocode: for l; s=0; for r>=l: s+=A[r]; if s==B: return; if s>B: break
solutions.story: Acceptable for small N; not for N=1e5.

solutions.label: Optimal — Two Pointers (positives only)
solutions.plain: Expand r; shrink l while sum > B.
approach: l = 0; long sum = 0.
For r = 0..N−1: sum += A[r]; while (sum > B && l <= r) sum −= A[l++].
If sum == B → return A[l..r]; else continue.
Return [-1].
solutions.pseudocode: l=0,s=0; for r: s+=A[r]; while s>B: s-=A[l++]; if s==B: return l..r
solutions.story: Optimal for positive arrays. Use long for the sum to avoid overflow.

data.footer: First subarray with sum = 5 using two pointers.

script.label: SETUP
script.overlay: Why two pointers OK? All elements positive → expanding r only grows sum; shrinking l only shrinks it; both monotonic.
